facts.fact: The IVC is the earliest known urban culture of the north-western Indian subcontinent.
The IVC is one of the world's first three civilizations, alongside Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt.
The IVC flourished from about 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE.
The IVC is dated by radiocarbon dating.
Fertile soil, a favourable climate and distinct landscapes aided the growth of the IVC.
The IVC is called the Harappan Culture because Harappa was the first site excavated (its type site).
The IVC is also called the Indus–Sarasvati Civilization.
Later discoveries such as Kalibangan, Lothal and Rakhigarhi showed the same Harappan characteristics.
The Indus civilization grew from settlements practising irrigated agriculture on the Mesopotamian model.
The Harappan civilization is divided into four phases: Pre-Harappan, Early, Mature and Late Harappan.
The Mature (urban) Harappan phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE (NCERT).
The Early Harappan phase is dated c. 3300–2600 BCE.
The Late Harappan phase is dated c. 1900–1300 BCE.
Older textbooks (R. S. Sharma / old NCERT) date the mature phase to c. 2500–1750 BCE.
The IVC was a Bronze Age (Chalcolithic) culture that used copper and bronze.
Iron was unknown to the Harappans; it appears only around 1000 BCE.
The Harappans knew copper, bronze, gold, silver, tin and lead.
Moisture-loving plants and animals on the seals suggest a fairly moderate ancient climate, though the region is arid today.
Annual Indus floods left rich alluvial soil on the plains bordering the river.
Charles Masson was the first to come across Harappa, which he identified as Sangala of Alexander's time.
Alexander Cunningham, first Director-General of the ASI, is called the father of Indian archaeology.
John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of the Indus civilization in 1924.
Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa (1921).
Rakhaldas (R. D.) Banerjee excavated Mohenjo-daro (1922).
R. E. M. Wheeler introduced stratigraphic excavation at Harappa in 1947.
The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was set up in 1861.
The IVC covered about 1,299,600 sq km (~1.3 million sq km).
The IVC covered a larger area than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia.
The IVC lay in the river basins of the Indus and the Ghaggar–Hakra.
The IVC extended into Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, Balochistan and a coastal strip of Gujarat.
The northernmost IVC site is Manda (Jammu, on the Chenab).
The easternmost IVC site is Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh).
The westernmost IVC site is Sutkagendor (Balochistan).
The southernmost IVC site is Daimabad (Maharashtra).
Older texts give the southern limit as Bhagatrav/Malwan in Gujarat instead of Daimabad.
Gujarat has the largest number of Harappan sites in India.
Over 1,000 Harappan sites have been identified (about 1,500 today).
Harappa lies on the Ravi river.
Harappa is in the Sahiwal (old Montgomery) district of Punjab, Pakistan.
Harappa had granaries — two rows of six granaries near the river.
Harappa was a gateway city and a meeting point of several routes.
Harappa yielded sandstone statues of human anatomy, including a red sandstone male torso.
Bullock carts (models) are among the Harappa finds.
The source text lists a stone dancing Nataraja among Harappa's finds.
Cemetery R-37 at Harappa shows coffin burial.
Cemetery H (Harappa/Punjab) is a Late Harappan culture.
The source text dates Harappa to 2600–1900 BCE.
Harappa had workers' quarters near its granaries.
Mohenjo-daro lies on the Indus river.
Mohenjo-daro is in the Larkana district of Sindh, Pakistan.
Mohenjo-daro means 'Mound of the Dead'.
The Great Bath is found only at Mohenjo-daro.
Mohenjo-daro had a collegiate building and an assembly hall.
The Great Granary is the largest building of Mohenjo-daro.
The bronze Dancing Girl was found at Mohenjo-daro.
The unicorn seal is a Mohenjo-daro find.
Woven cotton was found at Mohenjo-daro.
The Pashupati (proto-Siva) seal was found at Mohenjo-daro.
The steatite 'Priest-King' bust was found at Mohenjo-daro.
The source text dates Mohenjo-daro to 2500–1700 BCE.
Mohenjo-daro is the largest Harappan site in Pakistan (older keys call it the largest overall).
Mohenjo-daro covers about 125 hectares.
A large Mohenjo-daro building once called a 'palace' yielded no rich finds.
Pashupati Mahadeva (proto-Siva) was the chief male deity of the Harappans.
The Pashupati figure sits in a yogic posture on a low throne, with three faces and two horns.
The Pashupati figure is surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a buffalo.
Two deer appear below the throne of the Pashupati figure.
NCERT cautions that identifying the Pashupati figure with Shiva is not straightforward.
Rakhigarhi is in Hisar district, Haryana.
Rakhigarhi is the largest Harappan site.
The source text places Rakhigarhi on the Sarasvati river (the Ghaggar plain).
Amarendra Nath (ASI) excavated Rakhigarhi.
Rakhigarhi had a mud-brick granary with a rammed-earth floor plastered with mud.
A seal bearing an alligator emblem was found at Rakhigarhi.
Rakhigarhi had burnt-brick houses and an effective drainage system.
An ancient-DNA study (2019) was carried out on a skeleton from Rakhigarhi's cemetery.
Dholavira lies on Khadir island in the Great Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
Dholavira was discovered by Jagat Pati Joshi (1967–68).
R. S. Bisht excavated Dholavira (1990–2005).
Dholavira became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 — India's 40th.
Dholavira was divided into a citadel, a middle town and a lower town.
Dholavira is famous for a cascading series of stone water reservoirs (water harvesting).
Dholavira is called a lake city or jala durga (water fort).
Dholavira used a lot of stone in its buildings.
Dholavira yielded redware and black-on-red ware ceramics.
Dholavira had burial grounds (a cemetery).
A stadium (ceremonial ground) was found at Dholavira.
Dholavira has a signboard of ten large Harappan signs.
UNESCO calls Dholavira the southern centre of the Harappan Civilization.
The source text dates Dholavira to 3500–1800 BCE.
Lothal lies in the Bhal region, Gulf of Khambhat (Ahmedabad district), Gujarat.
Lothal had a tidal dockyard — the earliest artificial dockyard.
Lothal is regarded as the sole port town of the IVC.
Lothal had a bead factory.
The fire god was revered at Lothal (fire altars).
Lothal gives early evidence of rice farming (rice husk) in South Asia.
Lothal was a city with an upper town and a lower town.
The source text notes coffin use in Lothal's graveyards.
Lothal pottery was made of black and red clay.
S. R. Rao excavated Lothal (1954).
Lothal lies on the Bhogava river, near the Sabarmati.
A Persian Gulf seal was found at Lothal — proof of sea trade.
An ivory measuring scale was found at Lothal.
Lothal has a joint (double) burial of a man and a woman.
The source text dates Lothal to 2400–1600 BCE.
Accurate weights and measures of various shapes were found at the Lothal dock.
The National Maritime Heritage Complex (NMHC) is being built at Lothal, Gujarat.
Kalibangan is in Rajasthan (Hanumangarh district) on the Ghaggar river.
Kalibangan was discovered by Amlanand Ghosh in 1953.
B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar excavated Kalibangan (1960–69).
Kalibangan has fire pits (fire altars).
Kalibangan has the earliest ploughed field (plough marks).
Kalibangan's field shows furrows at right angles — a double-cropping pattern.
Kalibangan had priest quarters.
A bronze bull was found at Kalibangan.
Kalibangan means 'black bangles'.
Kalibangan shows traces of an earthquake.
The source text dates Kalibangan to 3500–2500 BC.
Symbolic burials (no body) were found at Kalibangan.
Banawali (Haryana, Ghaggar) was excavated by R. S. Bisht in 1974.
Banawali yielded a terracotta toy plough.
Banawali shows a fortified town, terracotta figurines and cotton cultivation.
Banawali yielded good-quality barley.
Mitathal (Haryana) was excavated by Suraj Bhan (1968) and shows two Harappan phases and pottery kilns.
Surkotada (Kutch, Gujarat) was excavated by J. P. Joshi in 1964.
Bones reported as horse come from Surkotada (debated; may be wild ass).
Pot burial is associated with Surkotada.
Rangpur (Saurashtra, Gujarat) was excavated by M. S. Vats in 1931.
Rangpur yielded evidence of rice (rice husk).
Rangpur is the type site of the Late Harappan 'Rangpur culture'.
Bhagatrav (Gujarat, Kim estuary) was a Harappan port and bead/shell centre excavated by S. R. Rao (1953).
Desalpur (Kutch, Gujarat) was a fortified township found by P. P. Pandya (1963).
Rojdi (Gujarat, Bhadar river) is an agricultural settlement excavated by Gregory Possehl (1982).
Bagasra (Gulf of Kutch) shows a shell industry; excavated by V. H. Sonawane (1996).
Alamgirpur (Meerut, UP) on the Hindon was excavated by Y. D. Sharma (1958).
Alamgirpur yielded late Harappan pottery.
Sutkagendor (Makran coast, Balochistan) lies on the Dasht river and was found by Aurel Stein (1929).
Sutkagendor was a fortified trade post near the Arabian Sea linking Harappa and Mesopotamia.
Balakot (Las Bela, Balochistan; George Dales 1973) was a coastal shell-working settlement.
Daimabad (Ahmednagar, Maharashtra) lies on the Pravara river.
Daimabad yielded a bronze hoard — a chariot drawn by two oxen, an elephant, a rhinoceros and a buffalo.
Manda (Akhnoor, Jammu) lies on the Chenab river.
J. P. Joshi excavated Manda (1976–77).
J. P. Joshi is credited with Surkotada, Dholavira and Manda.
Chanhudaro (Sindh) was excavated by N. G. Majumdar (1931).
Chanhudaro had a bead-making factory (APPSC 2023).
Chanhudaro is the only Harappan city without a citadel.
An inkpot and lipstick were found at Chanhudaro.
A brick at Chanhudaro bears paw-prints of a dog chasing a cat.
Chanhudaro is a tiny craft settlement of under 7 hectares.
Ropar (Punjab, Sutlej) was the first Harappan site excavated after Independence (Y. D. Sharma, 1953).
At Ropar a dog was buried with its master.
Ropar lies on the Sutlej.
Y. D. Sharma excavated both Ropar and Alamgirpur.
Balathal (Udaipur, Rajasthan) gave India's earliest skeleton with leprosy.
Bhirrana (Fatehabad, Haryana) claims the oldest Harappan layers and has a 'dancing girl' scratched on a potsherd.
Kot Diji (Sindh) is an Early Harappan fortified town excavated by F. A. Khan (1955).
Amri (Sindh) shows pre-Harappan 'Amri culture' layers under Harappan ones.
Sothi (Rajasthan) is known for Early Harappan 'Sothi' pottery.
Nageshwar (near Dwarka, Gujarat) was a shell-working centre.
Shikarpur (Kutch) shows Early and Mature Harappan layers with shell bangles.
Allahdino near Karachi is a small unfortified Harappan village.
Shortughai (northern Afghanistan, Amu Darya) was a Harappan trading outpost near lapis lazuli mines.
Shortughai is the only Harappan site with traces of irrigation canals.
Mehrgarh (Kacchi plain, Balochistan; c. 7000 BCE) is the pre-Harappan root of the IVC.
Mehrgarh was excavated by Jean-François Jarrige (1974).
Mehrgarh's farmers grew einkorn wheat and six-row barley and lined baskets with bitumen.
Sohgaura is NOT a Harappan site — it is a Mauryan copper-plate inscription site (UPSC 2019).
Harappan cities followed a rectangular grid pattern with roads meeting at right angles.
The grid roads divided into smaller roads connected to lanes of individual houses.
Burnt (baked) mud bricks were used for construction.
Harappan bricks were standardised in a 4:2:1 ratio (length : breadth : thickness).
Buildings included dwelling houses, public buildings and public baths.
Cities were divided into a raised citadel to the west and a lower town to the east.
The citadel held granaries, administrative buildings, courtyards and pillared halls.
The lower town had small one-room quarters for workers and public baths.
Small house drains connected to larger drains running along the main roads.
Drains were loosely covered to allow regular cleaning.
Cesspits were placed at regular intervals along the drains.
The uniform layout and standard bricks over a vast area imply centralised civic planning.
Houses had wells and bathing platforms.
Harappan houses had no windows opening on the main street.
The Great Bath is about 12 m × 7 m and 2.4 m deep.
The Great Bath's bricks were set in gypsum mortar and sealed with bitumen; steps on the north and south.
Wheat and barley were the main Harappan crops.
Harappans also grew lentil, chickpea and sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice was rare.
Harappan fruits included pomegranates and bananas.
The Harappan diet included meat and fish.
Domesticated animals included cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig.
The Harappans were the first to produce cotton; the Greeks called it 'sindon'.
Terracotta plough models come from Cholistan and Banawali.
The bull on seals implies oxen were used for ploughing.
Harappan occupations included weaving, bead-making, metalwork and trade.
Beads were made of clay, stone, paste, shell and ivory.
The Harappans traded with the Persian Gulf and the Sumerians.
Seals and small objects of Mohenjo-daro have been found in Iraq (Mesopotamia, e.g. Ur).
Lapis lazuli was obtained through trade with Afghanistan.
Copper came from Khetri in Rajasthan.
Harappan trade was by barter — no coins were used.
Mesopotamian texts call the Indus region Meluhha.
Dilmun of the Mesopotamian texts is Bahrain.
Magan of the Mesopotamian texts is Oman, a copper source.
The red colour of carnelian beads was obtained by firing.
Specialised drills are known from Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.
Harappan gold jewellery was recovered mainly from hoards.
Harappan weights were made of chert, usually cubical and unmarked.
Harappan weights were binary in the lower range and decimal in the higher, in multiples of 16.
Spindle-whorls but no spinning wheels are found, so spinning was done at home (UPSC 2026).
Harappan clothes were mostly of wool and cotton.
Women wore a short skirt; men wrapped a long piece of cloth.
Women wore bracelets and necklaces of shells, gold and silver.
Men wore amulets for protection.
Children played with clay carts, dolls, rattles and marbles.
Puppets of animals and bird-shaped whistles were made.
Old people enjoyed gambling.
IVC society was predominantly secular, with religion not dominant (UPSC 2011).
No temples or palaces have been conclusively identified in the IVC.
The 'Priest-King' label is a Mesopotamian analogy and is not proven.
No royal tombs have been found, unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia.
Scholars debate a single state, several rulers, or an egalitarian society with no ruler.
The horse was absent or not central to Harappan life, unlike for the Rigvedic Aryans (UPSC 2017).
The cow is not represented on Harappan seals and terracotta art (UPSC).
Terracotta figurines of women are regarded as Mother Goddesses (fertility cult).
The Peepal tree was sacred to the Harappans.
The horned/humped bull was held sacred.
Phallus (lingam) and yoni worship are attributed to the Harappans.
Fire altars are found at Kalibangan and Lothal.
The source text lists three burial types: extended, symbolic and twin.
In extended burial the body was laid North–South.
Twin burial means two bodies in one grave (e.g. man and dog).
Grave goods in burials suggest a belief in life after death.
Harappan seals were mostly made of steatite, a soft stone found in river beds.
Seals of copper, gold, faience, ivory and terracotta were also found.
Seal shapes were square, triangular, rectangular and circular.
Most Harappan seals are square.
The Harappan script is pictographic and written from right to left.
Multi-line Harappan inscriptions are often boustrophedon (alternating direction).
The Harappan script is still undeciphered.
The script has about 375–400 signs; the longest inscription has about 26 signs.
The unicorn (one-horned bull) is the most common motif on Harappan seals.
Some seals show a half-man, half-animal figure, such as the Pashupati seal.
Seals were used mainly for trade, identification and educational purposes.
The swastika appears on some Harappan seals.
Harappan bronzes were cast by the cire perdue (lost-wax) technique.
The Dancing Girl stands in the tribhanga posture.
The Dancing Girl is made of bronze (UPSC 2025).
Terracotta (fire-baked clay) was used for toys, animal figures, miniature carts and wheels.
Two kinds of pottery are found: plain and painted.
Painted Red-and-Black pottery has a red background with black designs.
Pottery themes were trees, birds, animals and geometric patterns.
Harappan pottery was wheel-made.
Pottery served household, decorative and liquor-pouring purposes.
The bearded priest wears a shawl with trefoil patterns and has half-closed meditative eyes.
The 'Priest-King' is a steatite (stone) figure.
The Dancing Girl is in the National Museum, New Delhi; the Priest-King in Karachi.
The source text dates the fall of the Harappans to around 1500 BCE, the period of the Aryans' arrival.
One theory: a massive Indus flood drowned the cities.
One theory: eastward-moving monsoons brought destructive heavy rains.
One theory: invasion by the Aryans, a nomadic Indo-European tribe.
One theory: drying of the Saraswati from about 1900 BCE caused drought.
One theory: droughts led to famines.
One theory: a pandemic disease wiped out the people.
By 1800 BCE a cooler, drier climate and a tectonic event may have disrupted rivers.
The Harappans may have migrated east toward the Ganga basin.
There is no conclusive evidence for any single cause of decline.
Mortimer Wheeler blamed an Aryan invasion ('Indra stands accused').
John Marshall attributed the decline to repeated Indus floods.
Robert Raikes and George Dales proposed tectonic uplift that dammed the Indus.
H. T. Lambrick proposed a change in the course of the Indus.
Aurel Stein and A. N. Ghosh blamed a drier climate.
K. V. R. Kennedy proposed an epidemic (malaria).
Walter Fairservis proposed ecological imbalance.
George Dales rejected the Mohenjo-daro massacre idea ('The Mythical Massacre at Mohenjo-daro').
In the Late Harappan phase seals, script, standard weights and long-distance trade fade.
The Late Harappan phase is a de-urbanisation into rural settlements, not an abrupt collapse.
Late Harappan cultures were primarily Chalcolithic (stone and copper tools) and village-based (APPSC 2024).
Bhagwanpura (Haryana) is a Late Harappan site overlapping with Painted Grey Ware.
Jhukar (Sindh) is a Late Harappan culture.
By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in Cholistan were abandoned.
APPSC Mains 2023 asked about the survival and continuity of Harappan culture today (cotton, carnelian, shell bangles).
The Harappan reach into the Deccan is shown by Daimabad; no Harappan site lies in Andhra Pradesh.
